b: Of the innumerable dazzling moments in Robert Altman’s Nashville, there’s one that particularly testifies to the film’s enduring stature as a somehow ageless American time capsule. Barbara Jean (Ronee Blakley), a country star, collapses almost immediately upon arriving at the Nashville airport, in front of the gathered press. Later, her husband and manager, Barnett (Allen Garfield), sits by her hospital bed, eating fried chicken and discussing with her how they should handle the politics of thanking Barbara Jean’s replacement for an upcoming show. Barbara Jean is professionally, perhaps also sexually, threatened by the competition, and she insists that Barnett disregard a variety of social and professional obligations that he intends to see through whether or not she approves.

But, this being an Altman film, none of these subtexts are voiced directly, and seemingly inconsequential lines assert themselves on the rebound maybe 10 minutes after we’ve already moved on to another privileged moment in another set of characters’ lives. Considering this scene between Barbara Jean and Barnett a day later, you may wonder who’s emotionally abusing whom, and the most likely, and interesting, answer would characterize the relationship as unhealthy though weirdly nourishing, and inseparable from the professional and personal realms that the couple must so carefully, and so publicly, navigate.

In this scene, Altman tells you more in a few spare moments about the emotional texture of a showbiz marriage than most biopics manage over the course of their entire running times, and the miracle of Nashville resides in just how many similarly evocative and empathetic scenes Altman and his amazing cast manage to forge over the course of 160 minutes. Over the years, the director frequently compared his filmmaking to the painting of a large mural, with the actors he chose often functioning as both his paint and his found objects, and that isn’t a case of an artist’s poetic hyperbole. Rewatching Nashville is to be reminded of the sheer enormity of the film’s canvas, which offers a vision of America as a fabulously irreverent and destructive melting pot—a society spinning a farce of ever-expanding entitlement without any notion or expectation of its corresponding personal, political, and social costs.

Nashville doesn’t quite have the emotional fullness of later Altman films such as Short Cuts and The Company, as it was made at the height of its creator’s run of defiantly smart-ass epics. But people who criticize Nashville for its occasional glibness are mistaking empathy and theme for a default authorial tic. America was created by its irreverence, and later defined by it, and Altman understands his country and celebrates it while often mercilessly lampooning it. Nashville shows the tragedy of America to ultimately be a failure of self-consciousness, as the most heartbreaking moments show people’s delusions being casually obliterated by the grazing indifference of social life at large, as it’s actually lived.

The film is an untraditional musical that, like most musicals, offers a testament to the artistic transcendence that’s inherent in its very existence. We see glorious washed-up stars mixing with never-will-be’s, and then we see them take the stage to offer performances that often rise above the limitations of the platitudes they’re putting forth. Haven Hamilton (Henry Gibson) sings a song that, on the page, epitomizes the absurd ego of America, bragging that a country that’s lasted 200 years must be doing something right—never mind that 200 years isn’t a squirt of piss in the context of civilizations that have been around for millennia. But Hamilton’s conviction, not to mention the surprisingly engaging depth of his voice, spins the kitsch into a beautiful, unintentionally ironic ode to hyperbole. And Altman never shortchanges his characters’ transcendence; he doesn’t edit the musical numbers to pieces, allowing us to savor them.

There’s still quite a bit of mystery left within this film more than 50 years after its release, as it’s one of only a few American films that suggest the medium’s capacity to operate as a truly vast visual novel or, perhaps even more fittingly, as a visual counterpart to a concept album, with its refrains, choruses, and throughlines. Stunningly, it isn’t even Altman’s best film (that would be McCabe & Mrs. Miller), but Nashville is still the one that best embodies everything that was so freeing and generous and deceptively casual about Altman’s art, and it’s the film that best represents him as a uniquely American artist. This is a film you could proudly show to a person from another country with the proviso: This is America, for better and worse. This is everything right and wrong that the experiment of this country has led to, and will probably lead to.

Criterion’s 2013 Blu-ray of Nashville, created in 2K resolution from a 35mm interpositive, offered a revelatory image that may have inspired you to rethink your impression of Robert Altman’s aesthetic, which isn’t always noted for its visual bravura, and this new 4K digital restoration, presented in Dolby Vision HDR, only builds on that foundation. The themes and the characters aren’t the only embodiments of the film’s grandness, as the image is breathtakingly wide and elaborately detailed. Take note of the scene in the bus yard, which boasts colors that subtly suggest the American flag in a great throwaway joke. Such nuance abounds here, and grain is beautifully preserved, with no signs, to these eyes, of awkward digital revisions. The English 5.1 surround DTS-HD Master Audio soundtrack is clear, immersive, and rich in audible textures, not least in the musical performances captured live on location.

The “get” here remains the 2013 documentary, produced for Criterion, that rounds up many of the Nashville veterans, including actors Ronee Blakley, Keith Carradine, Michael Murphy, Allan Nicholls, and Lily Tomlin, screenwriter Joan Tewkesbury, assistant director Alan Rudolph, and Altman’s widow, Kathryn Reed Altman, for a terrific collection of interviews that discuss the staging of pivotal scenes with remarkable specificity. Altman’s audio commentary is fine, but the director tends to let the film play out uninterrupted. New fans looking for the director’s input are better advised to check out the three archival interviews that, taken together, offer a succinct portrait of how Altman’s presentation of his sensibilities to the press evolved over the years (the short answer: You get to see a great American artist perfect his outward performance as a Great American Artist). Behind-the-scenes footage, a demo of Carradine performing his songs from the film, the trailer, and a terrific essay by Molly Haskell round out the package, though, if one were to carp, it would’ve been nice to see more critical perspectives provided, given the heated critical debate that greeted the film upon its release in 1975.
Love it, hate it, or love it and hate it, Nashville is one of the most revealing portraits of America ever made, and it’s never looked or sounded this good.
